newsitem.title: BOSNIA: First foreign bank opens in post-war Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: First foreign bank opens in post-war Bosnia.

text.p: Turkey's government-owned Ziraat Bank has opened an office in Sarajevo and encountered the complexity of Bosnia's post-war economic system, manager Aysegul Topbas said on Tuesday.
"The economy could be more liberal and our computer experts are still trying to install the Bosnian accounting system in our computers," she told Reuters.
Bosnia is slowly rebuilding itself with foreign aid but monetary chaos still reigns in the country.
Bosnia's Serbs, Croats and Moslems use three different currencies and even in the Moslem-Croat federation the mutual payment system uses German marks.
Bosnia has yet to enact reforms needed to convert to a free market and open the country to foreign capital after decades of communist management as part of former Yugoslavia.
Some 48 banks are now registered in Bosnia and even though its peacetime economic development hardly justifies so many, there are prospects for profits, bankers say.
"We are willing to take the risks (of a volatile area)," Topbas told Reuters.
Ziraat's subsidiary bank in Sarajevo, with 10 million marks in founding capital, offers the same conditions to clients as Bosnian banks, she said.
"We provide a full international and domestic service to our clients, but we hope to be more competitive with higher interest rates on savings in future," Topbas said.

Six months deposits get a one percent monthly rate and money tied up for a year harvests a two percent monthly rate in Bosnia. The bank currently services about 30 Turkish trade companies and 100 individuals, Topbas said.
An automatic teller machine sits idle in the bank's newly decorated office, not connected but drawing curious looks from customers not accustomed to credit card business in Sarajevo.
"We'll start the machine in a couple of months," explained Topbas.
Ziraat's Sarajevo branch, with a staff of eight, including five Bosnian clerks fluent in Turkish, is taking a cautious approach to expanding across country.
"We'll see how things develop," the manager said.
